headline: NZ Unemployment Rises to 5.6% as Parliament Advances Climate Liability Bill
summary: Parliament debated rising unemployment, housing hardship and access to medicines as ministers defended the Government’s economic approach and faced questions over public resources and the Foreign Minister’s comments about China. During an extended sitting that continued into Thursday morning, MPs advanced several bills, including a contentious measure to bar climate-related tort claims. The day also exposed divisions over Treaty obligations, local democracy and employment protections.

topicSummaries.topic: Unemployment Rises to 5.6% as Parties Clash Over the Economy
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The unemployment rate affects household incomes and job prospects, while the debate highlighted competing claims about how quickly the economy may recover.
topicSummaries.content: Stats NZ figures for the April-to-June quarter showed unemployment rising from 5.4 to 5.6 percent, which Opposition MPs described as an 11-year high and higher than Treasury had forecast. Finance Minister Nicola Willis said 13,000 more people were employed than in March and average hourly earnings rose 1.1 percent, but the labour force grew faster; she also pointed to increased business confidence and hiring intentions as signs of possible future improvement. Labour MPs cited higher long-term unemployment and the increase in people out of work since the Government took office, while Willis argued that fast-tracked projects, investment incentives, tourism and trade policies would support job creation. The Speaker declined Labour MP Ginny Andersen’s request for an urgent debate on unemployment, citing earlier rulings that a continuing problem did not meet the test for an urgent debate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ginny Andersen (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: How can today’s unemployment rate, which is higher than Treasury had forecast, be a sign of economic growth?

keyExchanges.speaker: Nicola Willis (National)
keyExchanges.quote: What we have seen from the ANZ Business Outlook more recently, following what was undoubtedly a very difficult quarter, is that businesses have said that their hiring intentions have increased, their confidence has increased, and that their investments will increase.

topicSummaries.topic: Cold-Weather Homelessness and Seniors’ Access to Savings Raised
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The speeches focused on whether people can access shelter, warmth and their own money when they face homelessness or need higher levels of care.
topicSummaries.content: In the general debate, Green MP Tamatha Paul described rough sleepers and people without adequate bedding during a severe Wellington cold snap, urging donations to frontline organisations and arguing that basic shelter should not depend on charity. She cited accounts from local support workers about people struggling to find warmth and accommodation, while cautioning against speculation about the cause of a man’s recent death on the street. Labour MP Ingrid Leary separately criticised the Government’s plan for retirement village residents to wait up to 12 months for repayment of their capital after leaving a village. Leary said residents may need that money for care or other costs and advocated a three-month repayment period; the transcript records her criticism but no ministerial response in this debate.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tamatha Paul (Green)
keyExchanges.quote: As Pastor Joe said, this is the kind of weather that can kill someone.

keyExchanges.speaker: Ingrid Leary (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Every month that the Government has chosen when it could have chosen nine months—it’s chosen 12 to hang on to that money and let the operators have it—is a choice of choosing between the operators and the residents who need that money for higher levels of care or their families for funeral expenses when they exit the village, or for other things that they need during a cost of living crisis.

topicSummaries.topic: ACT Calls for a Seven-Year Plan to Narrow the Medicines Access Gap
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: Access to publicly funded medicines can affect whether patients receive treatment in New Zealand or have to seek alternatives overseas.
topicSummaries.content: ACT MP Todd Stephenson said New Zealand spends a smaller share of its health budget on medicines than the OECD average and claimed Australia funds 142 more medicines. He proposed allocating one percent of future increases in health spending to Pharmac, saying the approach could roughly triple Pharmac’s budget and close the gap with Australia in about seven years. Stephenson said ACT had written to other party leaders seeking support for the proposal; it was an appeal for cross-party backing, not a bill or policy decision adopted by the House.

keyExchanges.speaker: Todd Stephenson (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: What ACT has proposed, and what we’re going to be asking every party in this Parliament to consider, is a pathway to closing that medicines gap with Australia.

topicSummaries.topic: Luxon Defends Air Force Flight After National Party Fundraiser
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The exchange raised questions about the use of military aircraft and whether public resources were used in connection with party-political activity.
topicSummaries.content: Labour leader Chris Hipkins questioned Prime Minister Christopher Luxon about using an Air Force aircraft after attending a National Party fundraising event. Luxon confirmed the last event of his day was a National Party event, but said his schedule and an early appointment the next morning meant a commercial flight was not workable. He argued the aircraft was used sparingly and that the flight did not add a cost to taxpayers because the planes needed to fly and pilots needed training hours. The Speaker ruled that the Prime Minister could be questioned about matters relating to his role as Prime Minister.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Was he attending a National Party fund-raising event immediately before using the air force to fly back?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The last event—yes—was a National Party event.

topicSummaries.topic: Peters’ China Remarks Prompt Questions Over Ministerial Confidence
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The dispute put New Zealand’s relationship with China and the treatment of Chinese and migrant communities under parliamentary scrutiny.
topicSummaries.content: Green MP Lawrence Xu-Nan repeatedly asked Foreign Minister Winston Peters about remarks made during a general debate, including a comparison involving Chinese people and flatfish. Peters disputed the wording and argued that questions about comments made as New Zealand First leader belonged in a general debate; the Speaker said the Foreign Minister could be asked whether he agreed with a party leader’s statement. Prime Minister Christopher Luxon said the remarks were offensive and had hurt the Chinese-Kiwi community, but maintained confidence in Peters and said the relationship with China remained in good shape. Labour also questioned whether the Government had apologised to China; Luxon said it had not and that an apology was not needed.

keyExchanges.speaker: Chris Hipkins (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: Has the New Zealand Government, in any capacity, conveyed any form of apology to the Chinese Government for the Minister of Foreign Affairs’ recent comments that he as Prime Minister described as racist; if so, what form did that apology take?

keyExchanges.speaker: Christopher Luxon (National)
keyExchanges.quote: We don’t need to. No, we haven’t. The relationship is in good heart, as I’ve just said.

topicSummaries.topic: Climate Tort Liability Bill Advances Despite Opposition Objections
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill would prevent climate-related tort claims in New Zealand courts, including ending the ongoing Smith v Fonterra case, according to the debate.
topicSummaries.content: During the extended sitting, MPs agreed to both parts of the Climate Change Response (Tort Liability) Amendment Bill in committee, while opposition amendments were defeated; the committee reported progress, so the bill had not completed its passage. Justice Minister Paul Goldsmith said climate policy and emissions obligations should be set by Parliament and the executive, and argued that tort claims could create a parallel and contradictory regime and uncertainty for business. Labour and Green MPs said the measure would extinguish an active court case and restrict the ability of people to seek remedies for climate-related harm. Goldsmith said the bill’s transitional provisions would end Mike Smith’s expectation of continuing his case, while disputing that this amounted to retrospectivity; the bill also rules out compensation for affected parties.

keyExchanges.speaker: Camilla Belich (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: The bill extinguishes the litigation that Mike Smith has brought, and he has managed, since 2019, through numerous interlocutory actions, strike-out applications, and appeals, to get to the point where the Supreme Court said, “You’re allowed to argue it, and we’ll set it down for next year.”

keyExchanges.speaker: Paul Goldsmith (National)
keyExchanges.quote: Our view is that New Zealand’s regulatory approach to greenhouse gas emissions and climate change harm should be managed by Parliament and the executive.

topicSummaries.topic: Lifejacket Bill Would Require Wear on Recreational Craft Under 6 Metres
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposed rule shifts from carrying lifejackets to wearing them on small recreational craft, with the stated aim of reducing preventable drownings.
topicSummaries.content: MPs completed committee consideration of the Maritime Transport (Lifejackets on Recreational Craft) Amendment Bill and reported it without amendment; it had not yet received its final reading. The bill’s scope was widened during select committee consideration from people under 15 to all people on recreational craft under six metres while underway. Sponsor Shane Reti said evidence showed 161 fatalities among people over 15, compared with eight among children under 15, since 2015, and said the change could save lives. MPs also discussed how local bylaws would be aligned and the meaning of “underway”; Reti said the measure establishes a national baseline and that water-safety agencies would guide people on choosing a suitable lifejacket.

keyExchanges.speaker: Cameron Luxton (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: Is there a risk that we go too high by not just making this really targeted, really focused on the regulations, the things that people might look in, day in, day out, when they’re going out in their small boat, taking the kids out fishing—that kind of thing.

keyExchanges.speaker: Shane Reti (National)
keyExchanges.quote: This is not a request here tonight, in any shape or form, to take it any further.

topicSummaries.topic: Nelson Tenths Bill Advances Land Transfer and Abel Tasman Access Arrangements
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The bill gives effect to a resolution concerning land ownership while setting out how public access and conservation management will continue.
topicSummaries.content: The House committee agreed to an amendment to the Te Here ā Nuku (Nelson Tenths) Bill and reported it with amendment. The legislation gives effect to an agreement transferring legal ownership of specified land from the Crown to trustees for the benefit of descendants of the original owners, whose beneficial ownership the court recognised. The Government said the Department of Conservation would continue managing public access to parts of Abel Tasman National Park under a 25-year licence, with a review planned around year 22. MPs discussed overlapping interests and the status of the land; the Minister said the arrangement was a resolution of a trust-law dispute, not a Crown gift or a Treaty settlement.

keyExchanges.speaker: Rachel Boyack (Labour)
keyExchanges.quote: This isn’t a matter of the Crown gifting land to the trust, it’s a matter of that land having always been owned by the trust.

keyExchanges.speaker: Tama Potaka (National)
keyExchanges.quote: The court declared and acknowledged that the ownership in these lands was retained by the descendants of the original owners of those lands.

topicSummaries.topic: Community Housing and Regional Trust Bills Clear Second Readings
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The changes could let a South Island housing provider operate beyond its current boundary and allow an Eastern Bay trust to make grants for a wider range of community needs.
topicSummaries.content: Two private bills passed their second readings. The Ōtautahi Community Housing Trust (Trust Variation) Bill would allow the Christchurch-based provider to expand beyond Christchurch and Banks Peninsula, while amendments set out how assets should be handled if the trust is wound up; speakers from across parties supported the bill. The Trust Horizon (Trust Variation) Bill would broaden the Eastern Bay of Plenty trust’s grant-making powers beyond energy-related purposes while retaining energy as a key purpose. MPs said Trust Horizon held more than $200 million in assets and argued that the existing restrictions limited its ability to support local projects. Both bills still required further stages before becoming law.

topicSummaries.topic: Local Government Bill Sent to Select Committee Amid Debate Over Councillor Access
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposal concerns whether elected councillors can obtain the advice and information needed to make decisions and be held accountable by voters.
topicSummaries.content: The Local Government (Management of Local Authorities) Amendment Bill was referred to the Governance and Administration Committee after its first-reading debate resumed. Sponsor Stuart Smith said the bill would clarify elected members’ oversight of council management and address cases where councillors had used official-information requests to obtain information from their own councils. Labour, the Greens and New Zealand First supported referral for further scrutiny, while raising questions about the bill’s wording, its effect on council staff roles and its implications for relationships with Māori. The bill’s final provisions and outcome remain to be considered by the select committee.

keyExchanges.speaker: Andy Foster (New Zealand First)
keyExchanges.quote: I think the intent of the bill is right. There is an issue here. There’s a perception that there is an issue here, and we need to explore that.

keyExchanges.speaker: Oriini Kaipara (Te Pāti Māori)
keyExchanges.quote: The question before us today isn’t simply whether councillors should have greater authority over chief executives; the real question is this: will this bill lead to better outcomes for our people?

topicSummaries.topic: Employment Exit Negotiation Bill Debate Continues
topicSummaries.whyItMatters: The proposal could change how employers and employees negotiate an agreed departure, raising questions about choice and workplace protections.
topicSummaries.content: ACT MP Laura McClure opened the second-reading debate on the Employment Relations (Termination of Employment by Agreement) Amendment Bill, but the debate was interrupted and set down for resumption at the next sitting. McClure said the bill would let either party request a voluntary discussion about an agreed exit, with no agreement unless both sides consent; she said select committee changes included a formal request process and limits on repeat requests. She criticised Labour and Green objections, while opponents’ concerns in the committee report included the risk that employees could feel pressured to leave. No decision on the bill was reached in this sitting.

keyExchanges.speaker: Laura McClure (ACT)
keyExchanges.quote: This is all it actually does. It is what actually happens now when we go down the track of without prejudice, after there has been a lot of hurt and a lot of time wasted.

conclusion: The House advanced measures on boating safety, housing and land ownership, but the unresolved climate-liability bill and disputes over jobs, public accountability and ministerial conduct left major political divisions on display.
